questions.question_text: A map shading counties darker for higher vaccination rates is a:
questions.explanation: Shading predefined areas by data intensity = choropleth. Dot density places dots; cartograms distort area by data value; isolines connect equal values. Map-type ID opens nearly every exam.

questions.question_text: A chain analyzing neighborhood income, foot traffic, and competitors before opening a store relies on:
questions.option_b: GIS — layering multiple spatial data sets
questions.explanation: Overlaying multiple spatial layers to answer a locational question is the defining function of GIS. GPS just gives coordinates; remote sensing collects imagery — both can feed INTO a GIS.

questions.question_text: A country with a wide-based population pyramid most likely has:
questions.option_a: low birth rates and aging population
questions.option_b: high birth rates, young population, high dependency ratio
questions.explanation: A wide base = many children = high CBR, typical of stage 2. Read pyramids bottom-up: base width is fertility, top width is longevity. Option A describes the inverted shape.

questions.question_text: In the Demographic Transition Model, the stage 2 population explosion occurs because:
questions.option_b: death rates fall while birth rates stay high
questions.explanation: Stage 2 growth comes from the GAP: mortality drops fast with public health, but fertility norms change a generation later. Birth rates don't rise — they just haven't fallen yet.

questions.question_text: A family leaves Venezuela (economic collapse) for Miami's Venezuelan community. The Miami pull illustrates:
questions.option_b: chain migration to an ethnic enclave
questions.explanation: Migrants follow networks — family and community ties lower the costs and risks of relocation (chain migration), which is why immigrant populations cluster rather than spread evenly.

questions.question_text: East Asian and European baby bonuses and parental-leave expansions respond to:
questions.explanation: TFR below ~2.1 means each generation shrinks — fewer workers supporting more retirees. Pronatalist incentives rarely restore replacement fertility, which is why immigration becomes the other lever.

questions.question_text: K-pop spreading first to cosmopolitan cities worldwide via social media exemplifies:
questions.explanation: Jumping between major nodes before filling in = hierarchical. Contagious spreads like a wave to adjacent areas; relocation requires migrants physically carrying the trait. Trace the PATH.

questions.question_text: Fast-food chains in India serving paneer burgers instead of beef illustrate:
questions.option_b: glocalization — global brands adapting to local preferences
questions.explanation: Global standardization meets local religious norms → hybrid adaptation. Globalization rarely produces pure homogenization; the exam rewards recognizing the LOCAL modification of global flows.

questions.question_text: Belgium, with distinct Flemish and Walloon regions under one government, is a:
questions.explanation: One sovereign state containing multiple nations = multinational state. The Kurds are the reverse — a stateless nation across several states. Nation = people; state = sovereign territory.

questions.question_text: Devolution differs from disintegration in that devolution:
questions.option_b: transfers some central powers to regional governments while the state stays intact
questions.explanation: Devolution is power-sharing downward — often a pressure valve AGAINST breakup (Scotland, Catalonia). It can precede disintegration if demands escalate, but the two aren't the same.

questions.question_text: In the Von Thünen model, dairy and market gardening locate nearest the city because:
questions.option_b: their products are perishable and transport costs dominate
questions.option_d: land is cheapest near the center
questions.explanation: The model trades land rent against transport cost: perishables (pre-refrigeration) must minimize distance, outbidding other uses for expensive close-in land. Land is most EXPENSIVE near the center.

questions.question_text: The Green Revolution raised food production primarily through:
questions.option_b: high-yield seeds, chemical fertilizers, and irrigation
questions.explanation: HYV wheat and rice plus the chemical-irrigation package multiplied yields on EXISTING land, at the cost of water depletion, runoff, and debt for small farmers who couldn't afford inputs.

questions.question_text: Rising rents in a renovated downtown displacing low-income residents as wealthier newcomers arrive is:
questions.explanation: Reinvestment + class turnover in central neighborhoods = gentrification (revitalization and displacement are the same process). Redlining is the opposite-era policy of denying loans to minority areas.

questions.option_a: land values and density decline with distance from the CBD
questions.option_b: all urban land costs the same
questions.option_c: suburbs have taller buildings than downtowns
questions.explanation: Accessibility premium: businesses outbid others for central locations, so land price falls with distance — and expensive central land gets built UP. Density gradients are the curve's signature.

questions.question_text: A brand designing in Paris, manufacturing in Bangladesh, and offshoring service to the Philippines illustrates:
questions.option_b: the new international division of labor
questions.explanation: High-value functions stay in the core; labor-intensive production moves to the low-wage periphery; services offshore to English-speaking middle countries. The NIDL is the signature of globalized supply chains.

questions.question_text: Wallerstein's world-systems theory differs from Rostow's stages by arguing:
questions.option_a: all countries pass identical stages independently
questions.option_b: development and underdevelopment are linked — the core extracts value from the periphery
questions.explanation: Rostow: every country climbs the same ladder alone. Wallerstein: the ladder IS the relationship — core wealth and peripheral poverty are co-produced. The semi-periphery shows mobility, killing option D.

questions.question_text: Why can GNI per capita mislead as a development measure?
questions.option_b: it hides internal inequality and ignores health, education, and gender gaps
questions.explanation: An average masks extremes, and money metrics miss wellbeing — which is why HDI bundles income with life expectancy and schooling, and GII adds gender. Composite indices exist because single metrics mislead.
